source.title: Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers
source.authors: Kristóf Váradi; Márk Marosi; Peter Antal

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests sparse-feature recovery and feature stability in a molecular transformer using SAE-specificity, reconstruction, and stability measurements, rather than the original toy-model method. The molecular-transformer setting also extends the evidence to a new domain.
record.gate_note: The paper measures chemically aligned SAE features, reconstruction fidelity, and feature stability across dictionary sizes, layers, and augmented SMILES. SAE downstream prediction and steering results are not rows here: they measure task performance or induced generation changes, not whether SAE features are canonical representation units. Cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study applies SAEs to a new kind of system, a 25M-parameter SMILES transformer. It reports how well SAE features recover chemical fragments compared with dense, PCA and random-rotation bases (V4). It also reports how well features match across dictionary sizes and how faithfully the SAEs reconstruct activations (V5). It does not reproduce the toy-model method, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that ReLU SAEs extract chemically meaningful fragment detectors that beat dense and PCA bases on specificity, and that SAE features help on downstream tasks. They find cross-size feature stability highest in early layers (L1), with deeper layers showing high mean alignment but lower one-to-one recovery. They attribute that gap tentatively to feature splitting or greater polysemanticity, and leave it to future work.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses ReLU SAEs and molecular-transformer feature screening, fidelity, and stability analyses; it does not reproduce the Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer depth, SAE expansion factor, and canonical versus augmented SMILES affect feature stability; reconstruction fidelity also varies by layer and dictionary size.

fits_no_version.finding: Agreement between SAE active-feature sets for canonical versus augmented SMILES is high at L0 (Jaccard ~0.94–0.99) and drops with depth and with dictionary width at deep layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in early layers are invariant to input string order; deeper-layer features are path-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Remaining valence is linearly decodable (probe accuracy 99.08% at L3), and steering along the probe direction shifts bond-order logits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Chemical quantities in molecular transformers are represented as linear directions.

record.problems: The mechanistic and SAE analyses focus on a single 25M-parameter molecular transformer. Cross-dictionary comparison is not a test across independent SAE random seeds. Feature alignment and reconstruction do not prove features are complete or canonical; the paper itself notes deeper-layer variability and the need for further feature elicitation.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix Table 11 reports specificity for many additional fragments; only four representative fragment conditions are retained here. Appendix Table 10's 4x and 8x reconstruction conditions are omitted; 16x results across layers are retained. Downstream prediction and steering outcomes are omitted because they do not directly measure feature recovery or canonicality.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions.
All of it: no alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Feature spread across neurons in general LLMs; tested only at layer 3 of one molecular transformer.
Stability across SAE random seeds or architectures; whether features are canonical beyond cross-size matching; feature splitting is suggested but not verified.
All of it: no 1-D versus multi-dimensional comparison.

missing.what: Random-rotation and PCA baseline columns for fragment specificity, including fragments where SAE falls below them (Isopropyl 0.20 vs 0.49, Ketone 0.18 vs 0.44, Tert-Butyl 0.18 vs 0.32).
Strongest SAE fragment detectors not in the rows: Chloro-Aromatic 0.46 vs 0.02, Nitrile 0.44 vs 0.01–0.02, Fluoro-Aliphatic 0.42 vs 0.06–0.09.
Reconstruction fidelity for 4x and 8x SAEs (e.g., L3 4x ΔCE 0.103, L4 4x 0.105), which shows how completeness depends on dictionary size.

record.verdict_notes: Dense specificity is 0.00±0.00 for every fragment, which suggests a degenerate baseline; random and PCA are the meaningful comparisons. The text's claim that SAEs 'consistently' beat PCA is not borne out for several fragments in Table 11. The stability analysis compares dictionary sizes, not seeds, so it does not address the seed non-identifiability the authors cite (Paulo & Belrose). Steering and downstream-task results were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test superposition, feature overlap geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular geometry in overcomplete toy networks.
Does not test whether polysemanticity results from capacity competition or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not test alternative causes of polysemantic neurons as evidence for or against superposition.
Tests recovery of chemically meaningful sparse features in one molecular transformer, not feature distribution in general LLMs or across model families.
Tests reconstruction fidelity and some feature stability across dictionary sizes and SMILES orderings; does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

relationships.condition: Layer 3, fragments such as fluoro-aromatic and benzene, versus random and PCA bases
relationships.reason: SAE max specificity 0.42 and 0.24 exceeds random/PCA (0.03, 0.11–0.13), so sparse fragment detectors are recoverable (T11-fluoroaromatic, T11-benzene).
relationships.display_finding: SAE maximum specificity for fluoro-aromatic and benzene fragments was 0.42 and 0.24, above random (0.03) and PCA (0.11–0.13) bases, so sparse fragment detectors were recoverable.

source_check.condition: Layer 3, fragments such as fluoro-aromatic and benzene, versus random and PCA bases

relationships.condition: Layer 3, fragments such as amide and urea (also isopropyl, ketone, tert-butyl in Table 11)
relationships.reason: SAE is below random/PCA for amide (0.22 vs 0.49) and only modestly above for urea (0.23 vs 0.14). This contradicts the text's 'consistently higher' claim (T11-amide, T11-urea).
relationships.display_finding: The SAE scored below the random/PCA baseline for amide (0.22 vs 0.49) and only modestly above it for urea (0.23 vs 0.14), contrary to the paper's own claim of consistently higher scores.
